READOUT Source channels — which one carries your signal?

The three channels of the image as loaded, before any swap. With a full-spectrum sensor behind a filter stack, which channel actually holds the IR or UV response depends on the stack, not on convention — so read it here rather than inferring it from the swapped result. The mean is the channel's average level: a channel sitting near black is mostly noise, and swapping it into a visible slot will amplify that noise.

READOUT Raw sensor data (experimental, diagnostic only)

The tool works from the camera's embedded preview above, which is already demosaiced and white-balanced. This looks past that, into the actual sensor plane inside the RAW file — the Bayer colour pattern, the black level, the as-shot white balance — as groundwork toward reading raw pixels directly. It is reporting only, right now: nothing here changes what you see or export.

02 Match Your Filter
UV Presets
IR Presets
RGB Channel Swap

A measured Aerochrome transform from Fedia, applied at the start of the workflow — it stands in for the channel swap, so white balance set afterwards still means what you set it to. On or off rather than a blend: it is a specific measured look, and a partial mix of it is not a weaker version of that look, just a different one.

A swap moves light between channels carrying very different amounts of it, so it changes brightness as a side effect of changing hue — foliage lands near two thirds, sky nearer one and a half. This holds the original brightness so frames stay comparable. Where the new hue cannot physically carry it — a saturated red turning blue would need almost three times white — it eases off rather than clipping.

Holds the brightness a pixel had before the swap. Where the new hue physically cannot carry it — a saturated red becoming blue would need nearly 3× — it recovers as far as the gamut allows and eases off rather than clipping.

03 White Balance
Pre-WB: Not set
Post-WB: Not set

Temperature: cool ← → warm · Tint: green ← → magenta. Applied after the picker, so use these to push a deliberate cast on top of a neutral result. The range runs to ±300 — beyond ±100 is further than most converters allow, for infrared files a picker alone cannot bring back.

Calibrate matrix from real patches

Photograph a few known-colour patches under your own filter stack, tap each one, and solve the matrix from measurement instead of a preset guess.

A tight fit through very few, very different patches can demand an extreme gain on one channel — tap a shadow and ask it to become white, for instance — and that gain amplifies the source image's own noise right along with the colour, which is what shows up as heavy grain. Smoothing trades a little fit accuracy for a lot less of that. Raise it if a solve comes out grainy; 0 fits the patches exactly, for when you know that's what you want.

04 Light

Highlights negative recovers what is still there near white; shadows positive lifts detail out of the dark. Neither can bring back a channel that clipped in camera — once it reads 1.0 there is nothing left to find.

Vignette

Centre: 0.50, 0.50 (default)

Positive brightens the corners — the usual correction. Negative darkens them instead, for adding a vignette rather than removing one. Spread is the radius left completely untouched before the correction begins, so this can stay a corner fix rather than a change across the whole frame; falloff shapes how sharply it grows once past that radius.

05 Colour
120° = Aerochrome swap

Trades brightness for richer colour where a hue can't have both.

Tri-tone merge

Three hue-rotated copies of the image, each auto-levelled on its own histogram, combined by taking the brightest of the three in each channel. A rebuild of the Aerochrome Photoshop action, whose look came from exactly this — layers at +118, +80 and +149 merged with Lighten. Defaults are the action's own values.

Split toning

Two tints crossing over between dark and bright. Added as chroma in OKLab, so it colours without lifting or dropping brightness. This is the one look a channel matrix cannot produce, because a matrix treats every pixel the same regardless of how bright it is.

Defringe

Removes the purple/magenta halos IR lenses leave on high-contrast edges. It smooths colour only — edge sharpness is unaffected. Start low; too much desaturates fine detail.

LUT (.cube) — optional colour grade (live)
No LUT loaded — a film-style grade layered on top of the channel swap, shown live in the preview.

Export format

Batch — apply this look to many files

Processes every file with the settings currently on screen and returns one .zip. Files are handled one at a time and never touch the preview, so your current image and adjustments are left exactly as they are. RAW files use their embedded preview, same as loading one normally.
